part_title: Choosing Traditional Rules Instead of Machine Learning
review_basis: Original AIF Module 03 WebP slides 62–62 individually viewed and narrated in their actual diagram order, including numeric examples and bottom decision cues.

scenes.title: When machine learning is not the right solution
scenes.narration: This slide is a decision lesson: use the simplest dependable tool that solves the actual problem. On the left is a deck with five red cards, three blue cards, and two yellow cards. That gives ten cards altogether. To calculate the exact probability of drawing a blue card, count three blue cards out of ten: three divided by ten is zero point three, or thirty percent. A few clear lines of traditional code can compute that result exactly and repeatably. Now look at the centre illustration. A machine learning model trained on examples might predict approximately zero point two eight. Such a result is an estimate learned from data, and even a well-trained model can be wrong. There is no reason to introduce an estimation error for arithmetic we already know how to do exactly. The right panel shows a large language model saying about zero point two five. A language model may generate a plausible explanation but is not a substitute for a verified calculation. Here the exact count is available, so use deterministic arithmetic rather than asking a generative model to guess. The bottom takeaway distinguishes problems with explicit rules from problems where complex patterns must be learned and approximate answers are acceptable. A spam classifier may benefit from machine learning because language patterns vary. Computing a known tax formula or a fixed card ratio typically needs ordinary rules, plus appropriate validation. Final decision question: what would you choose for this exact card probability, a chatbot or basic arithmetic? Basic arithmetic, because the rules and values are known.
